newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanians cheer Clinton in "Liberty Plaza".
newsitem.headline: Romanians cheer Clinton in "Liberty Plaza".

text.p: Tens of thousands of Romanians, many of them veterans of hard-fought battles to overthrow Communism, poured into a central Bucharest square on Friday to acclaim U.S. President Bill Clinton.

Teenagers and pensioners waited for hours in scorching sun for a glimpse of Clinton, who picked University Square to address the crowd -- highlight of an eight-hour visit, the first to Romania by a U.S. leader in 22 years.
Waving small Romanian tricolors and the stars-and-stripes, the crowds burst into applause and cheers as Clinton climbed onto a podium alongside Romanian President Emil Constantinescu.

There was scant disappointment over Romania's failure to gain early entry to NATO at this week's Madrid summit, where at Clinton's insistence, the Alliance asked only Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic as the first new members.
"I feel the same hope as I did when I was here during the revolution, nearly eight years ago," said Marin Balaceanu, 49, a former saxophone player turned civil rights activist.
"Our time will come later, I'm sure it will come," said Lucian, 17, who had travelled with friends from Brasov in the Carpathian Mountains north of the capital to greet Clinton.
Romanian leaders acknowledged the Madrid setback and took solace in the fact that the summit singled out Romania, along with Slovenia, as leading candidates for future enlargement.
Clinton won further cheers by calling the square "Liberty Plaza" -- homage to hundreds of students shot by police in the dying days of Communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu's regime.
Some 1,500 people were killed across Romania during the 1989 revolt. Ceausescu was ousted and shot on Christmas Day.
On Friday, teenagers on roller skates circled around police lining the square, while rock and country music bands entertained crowds hours ahead of Clinton's arrival.

Parents with toddlers perched on their shoulders brushed past people walking well-groomed dogs, including some with American flags pinned to their collars. Soft drinks flowed freely from tanker trucks parked nearby.
The crowd was easily the largest in the square since elated voters converged on the spot after Constantinescu defeated ex-Communist Ion Iliescu in last November's presidential polls.
Many will have remembered when the square was the scene of bloody confrontation, even after Ceausescu's demise.
Six months after his execution, vigilante miners with clubs beat up students who had camped there for weeks to denounce Iliescu and other leftists who took the dictator's place.
"This place is now a symbol of liberty, a place where people died for freedom. It's also a symbol of democracy," said Constantinescu, a bearded academic with no political career under Communism.
Not everyone shared the crowd's enthusiasm.
One poster held aloft proclaimed in English: "Bill, don't sell us to the Russians."
Another group of youngsters in black leather, their ears and noses pierced by rings, sulked over the Madrid decision.
"Bill's not my chum. He didn't take us into NATO," said one 15-year-old girl identifying herself only as "Killer".
